units.text: Assessment of socioeconomic and ecological impacts on integrated rice cultivation in Africa: a systematic review and meta-analysis
Introduction

Integrated rice-fish (RF) culture has been practiced in many countries in the world, especially in Southeast Asia for centuries (Dubois et al., 2019;Halwart & Gupta, 2004).Early review on RF culture has shown that it was practiced on six continents globally since the mid-1900s, including Africa (Dadzie, 1992;FAO, 1957;Halwart & Gupta, 2004).The initial integrated culture started with capturing and raising of wild fish in the system by allowing the fish to enter the rice field (Koide et al., 2015).Since then, several experimental trials have been carried out and RF farms were established with successful results reported from increasing in income generation, rice yield and fish growth rate to ecological enhancement through implementation of integrated RF in different agroecological zones in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) (Akegbejo-Samsons, 2010;AquaFish CRSP, 2011;Dossou-Yovo et al., 2021;Freed et al., 2023;Niaré & Kalossi, 2014;Ofori et al., 2005;Sanni & Juanich, 2006;WorldFish, 2023).Several literatures have reported contribution of integrated RF culture to the household income in Africa with one to two cycles of rice and fish harvest per year, culturing significantly valuable fish species such as tilapia, carps, and catfish (Akegbejo-Samsons, 2010;Freed et al., 2023;Kamagaté et al., 2021;Onoh et al., 2020;Rasowo et al., 2010).Such integrations of crops and animals in the water system are unique and have been found to significantly improve nutrition and alleviate poverty in rural communities (Atkins et al., 2020;Halwart & Gupta, 2004).It also provides an additional source of income for farmers (Atkins et al., 2020) compared to the culture of rice or fish alone (Yaro, 1999).

With rice being the staple food source for many people, and fish being the most important and cheapest source of animal protein, the integration of RF farming is seen as a system with multiple benefits to food production, nutrition, and income generation (Desta et al., 2015;Onoh et al., 2020).However, the scarcity of inorganic fertilizers, the decline in soil fertility, and low rice yield are major obstacles impeding efforts to improve rice production and fulfill the needs of a growing population in many African countries.While the rice yields in the monoculture system have increased mainly from the increasing use of fertilizers and pesticides as well as the use of improved rice varieties in Africa, the demand for rice is still higher than the local supply.Currently, the local rice production accounts for around 55% of total rice consumption, with the difference being filled by rice imports from Asia at a cost of $30 million USD annually for SSA (FAOSTAT, 2023).Therefore, to help secure food supplies, improve rural economies, and to ensure a sustainable farming practice, RF integration is considered as an important system in the rice-growing areas in the world (Frei & Becker, 2005;Halwart, 2006;Halwart & Gupta, 2004;Hu et al., 2016).

The benefits of integrated RF system to the environment, society and economic are certain, as cited in the literatures (Desta et al., 2015;Freed et al., 2023;Kamagaté et al., 2021;Mortillaro & Dabbadie, 2018;Onoh et al., 2020).These benefits include the improvement of soil fertility and water quality, which in return increases rice yield, fish growth, productivity, and profitability (Bello et al., 2020;Desta et al., 2014Desta et al., , 2015;;Onoh et al., 2020;Serrem et al., 2015).The co-culture practices are known to improve nutrient and increase water use efficiency by reducing the use of chemical fertilizers and sustainable utilization of irrigation water (Baba et al., 2013;Dossou-Yovo et al., 2021).

Previous studies have shown that integrated ricefish (RF) systems significantly reduce the use of pesticides and herbicides, offering greater economic and ecological benefits compared to rice monoculture (Arunrat & Sereenonchai, 2022;Dwiyana & Mendoza, 2008;Hu et al., 2016;Nnaji et al., 2010).Research indicates that rice farmers in Africa apply a wide range of pesticides to manage pests such as birds, rodents, insects, crustaceans, and other organisms (Sankoh et al., 2016).However, the ineffective and improper use of these chemicals has been found to negatively impact human health and the environment (Ndayambaje et al., 2019;Sankoh et al., 2016), and has led to reduced fish and rice yields with increased pesticide usage.Integrated RF farming can mitigate these adverse effects by reducing pesticide use (Berg & Tam, 2018), serving as a form of biological control to combat harmful pests and diseases (Akegbejo-Samsons, 2010;Koide et al., 2015).Regarding weed management in irrigated rice systems in Sub-Saharan Africa, integrated RF farming could provide an effective weed control strategy, reducing herbicide use through the consumption of weeds by fish and minimizing the long-term pollution impact of chemical use on soil properties and the environment in rice fields (Ibrahim et al., 2021;Krupnik et al., 2012).Besides that, feces excreted by the fish provide nutrients in the culture system leading to increase in soil productivity and nutrient availability for rice plants (Akegbejo-Samsons, 2010;Bello et al., 2020;Misau et al., 2015).Other gains from integrated RF include additional income of the farmers from the production of both rice and fish, compared with rice or fish production alone (Mortillaro & Dabbadie, 2018).

Despite many studies showing advantages of integrated RF system compared with the monoculture, several factors were observed affecting the adoption of integrated RF in Africa.Several literatures have documented the existing constraints of RF system adoption in Africa, and this ranged from governance and institutional support to lack of financial capital and labour, training opportunities, land ownership, access to sufficient water, quality fish feed and fry, reduced in soil fertility, farm technical and management issues, and climate variability (Akegbejo-Samsons, 2010;Dossou-Yovo et al., 2021;Freed et al., 2023;Kamagaté et al., 2021;Mortillaro & Dabbadie, 2018;Niaré & Kalossi, 2014).Presently, the issues on soil fertility and climate change have become a major concern affecting the rice yield and fish production in Africa, leading to decrease in farmers income and food supply in the region (Akpoti et al., 2022;Dossou-Yovo et al., 2020, 2022;Johnson et al., 2023;Muringai et al., 2022;Uwimana et al., 2018;van Oort & Zwart, 2017).Compared to the rice monoculture, integrated RF farming is identified as a promising innovative climate-smart agriculture (CSA) technology to address the existing gaps of lower rice yield and fish production in Africa (Dossou-Yovo et al., 2021).To date, there has been no research carried out to comparatively assess integrated RF and rice monoculture and fish monoculture systems in Africa.This study aimed to review the agronomic and economic performances of integrated RF farming and identify the constraints and enabling conditions for large-scale adoption in SSA.Specifically, a systematic review was carried out to assess the effect of integrated RF system on fish growth rate, rice yield, water quality, income, and soil properties in Africa.The data collected were used for quantitative meta-analysis of the RF integration in Africa.
Materials and methods
Data collection

A systematic literature review was used to search papers published from January 1999 to December 2023 that investigated the effects of integrated RF system on socioeconomic and ecological aspects in Africa.The socioeconomic part of the integrated RF culture covers fish, rice, water quality, soil properties, production costs, and income components affecting the social and economic aspects from practicing RF farming compared to the rice or fish monoculture.While the ecological part covers soil physicochemical, weeds, pests and diseases control, and aquatic organisms' components affecting the ecosystem aspects from integrated RF compared to the monoculture system.Relevant papers including grey literature were retrieved from the Google Scholar and Science-Direct database using combination of keywords, namely 'rice-fish, rice and fish, systems or integrated culture or co-culture', 'rice or grain yield', 'fish yield', 'fish growth ', 'soil properties', 'water quality', 'ecology', 'cost-benefit', 'economic', 'socio-economic', 'revenue', 'climate change', 'benefits', 'constraints', 'nutrient', 'efficiency', 'malaria', and 'Africa'.The titles, abstracts, and full text of relevant papers were reviewed to identify those that met the inclusion criteria.In total, out of the 995 papers screened, 23 studies were eligible for assessment.Out of this, 5 studies were included for the meta-analysis, with 30 identified paired data (comparison between integrated RF with rice or fish monoculture).Eighteen studies were excluded due to the unavailable data reported on the target variable in one of the treatments (integrated RF systems) and control group (rice or fish monoculture) (Figure 1).

The papers were screened according to the following criteria: (i) the experimental design included rice or fish monoculture as control and integrated RF system as treatment; (ii) the study reported at least one of the target variables (rice yield, fish growth rate, water quality, production cost, revenue, net income, soil properties, nutrient use efficiency, water use efficiency, plankton density, weeds, pests, and diseases, climate adaptation); (iii) for the same data from one study in different publications, the data were only recorded once; (iv) in a study that included one, two or more co-culture species besides integrated RF system, the study was considered as different observations and was excluded; (v) the language of the study was in English and French; and (vi) the study was conducted in African countries.
Meta-analysis

The number of selected studies included in the meta-analysis for the last twenty years in each country were illustrated in Figures 2 and 3.The meta-analysis was conducted as described by Hedges et al. (1999).The mean (X), standard deviation (SD), and sample sizes (n) of the target variables in each study were extracted.Corrected standardized between-group mean-difference or Hedges' g was used.If standard error (SE) was reported in the study instead of the SD, SD was calculated using the following equation:
SD = SE �� n √

The effect of integrated RF system on rice yield, fish growth rate and water quality were evaluated by the natural log response ratio (lnRR), as follows (Liu et al., 2023;Yu et al., 2023;Zhang et al., 2023):
ln (RR) = ln X t X c

where X t and X c represent the mean of the targeted variable in the treatment (integrated RF system) and control (rice or fish monoculture), respectively.Effect sizes were calculated using the weighted mixed effect model.The unweighted resampling methods using statistical software MetaWin 3.0 (4999 iterations) was used to estimate 95% confidence intervals (CIs) (Adams et al., 1997;Rosenberg, 2022;Zhang et al., 2023).To directly present treatment effects, the percentage changes of effect sizes were measured using [exp(lnRR)-1] × 100% (Cui et al., 2023;Liu et al., 2023).The effect sizes of integrated RF system were significant (p < 0.05) if the 95% confidence interval (CI) did not overlap with zero.The results showing the effect of integrated RF system on the targeted variables were presented in forest plots, bar graphs and matrix correlation, which were  created using 'ggplot2 ','dplyr','Hmisc' and 'corrplot' in R packages in R software (v. 4.3.2) (Team, 2022).
Results
Effects of integrated RF system on rice yield, fish growth rate and water quality

The integrated RF system demonstrated a significantly higher effect (p < 0.05) on fish growth rate (FGR), with an increase of 5.7% compared to rice or fish monoculture (Figure 4).Fish fingerlings, 150 days old, stocked in the RF system showed a substantial 30% increase in FGR compared to those in fish monoculture.Furthermore, the FGR was 7% higher in the RF system using the FARO60 rice variety compared to the integrated system using the FARO45 variety.The contents of dissolved oxygen (DO), pH, and phosphorus significantly increased by 129%, 10%, and 71%, respectively, in the integrated RF system compared to rice monoculture.The overall effect of the integrated RF system on rice yield showed no significant difference (p > 0.05) when compared to rice monoculture.
Effects of integrated RF system on total production cost, revenue, and net income

Overall, the integrated RF system increased production cost, revenue and net income compared to the rice monoculture with no significant differences found between the two culture systems (Figure 5).The average production cost, revenue and net income were found to increase by 95% (USD 203), 39% (USD 492) and 28% (USD 292), respectively in the integrated RF than in the rice monoculture.
Factors contributing to rice yield and water quality increase in integrated RF system

Table 1 showed the correlation analyses results between water quality parameters and rice yield in the integrated RF plots.Strong positive correlations were observed between water pH and water dissolved oxygen on one hand and water pH, water dissolved oxygen and rice yield on the other hand.Increase in rice yield in RF plots was associated with an increase in water pH and water dissolved oxygen.
Effects of integrated RF system on soil properties and environment

Soil properties, water use efficiency, nutrient use efficiency, weeds and pests and diseases control were reported to be improved with integrated RF system, as compared with rice monoculture.Soil organic carbon (SOC), total nitrogen (TN), and available phosphorous (P) increased by 43%, 39%, and 26% respectively in the integrated RF system compared with the rice and fish monoculture (Table 2).Water use efficiency (WUE) enhanced in the integrated RF system due to reduced use of chemical fertilizers and pesticides (Table 2).Nutrient use efficiency (NUE) in the integrated RF system was improved due to increase in the nutrient content from fish organic waste which enhanced plant growth (Table 2).Weeds, pests, and diseases were reduced in the integrated RF system than in the rice monoculture (Table 2).Mosquito larvae density was reported to be reduced in the integrated RF (Table 2), thus potentially reducing the prevalence of diseases such as malaria, schistosomiasis, and worm infestations (Table 2).Incidence of rice stem-borers were significantly (p < 0.05) reduced in the integrated RF system compared with the rice monoculture (Table 2).Integrated RF was prioritized as one of the best solutions to increase productivity, adaptation to climate change, and increase soil carbon sequestrations in submergence rice systems in Mali (Table 2).
Factors affecting the adoption of integrated RF system in Africa

Land ownership, water supply problem, access to fish feed and fry, price and quality of fingerlings and fish feed, and lack of funding were the major constraints to the adoption of integrated RF (Table 3).Other factors limiting adoption of integrated RF included lack of training and labour, farm technical and farm management issues resulting in loss of rice and fish because of water use inefficiency and lack of protective grids for prevention of aquatic and terrestrial predators into the farming system, and fish theft (Table 3).
Discussion
Rice yield, fish growth rate and water quality response to integrated RF system

Results of the meta-analysis showed significant effects of the integrated RF on water quality (DO, pH and phosphorus level) and fish growth rate.Generally, the best DO and pH ranges for fish species are between 3 and 5 mg/L and 6.5-9, respectively, for fish growth and reproduction.This applies generally for warm water fish species such as tilapia and catfish.Lower of this range, the fish can still survive but will have an effect on its growth and reproduction.The higher DO level observed in the integrated RF than in rice monoculture could be due to the fish movements in the water column and the photosynthesis of phytoplankton in the pond water (Li et al., 2019;Osuigwe et al., 2007).Rice cultivation could also promote oxygen diffusion from the atmosphere to water through the waving of rice plants caused by the wind (Li et al., 2019).The correlation analysis showed a strong association between water pH and DO, which can be deduced by the correlation with growth and abundance of phytoplankton which were affected by pH (Li et al., 2019).A reduction in water pH of 6.7 in the RF system may promote the growth of phytoplankton, which in turn increases fish growth and production.Moreover, water pH and DO show a significant association with rice yield in the integrated RF (Table 1), which indicates that the water quality and presence of fish in the rice field does not affect rice yield (Hu et al., 2016;Ofori et al., 2005;Osuigwe et al., 2007).

The higher phosphorous level in the integrated RF system compared to rice monoculture was possibly due to the fish feces which recycled nutrients such as phosphorous (Jean-Renaud et al., 2016).This nutrient is taken up by rice plants and serves as natural fertilizers for the soil and water organisms.The close association between rice and fish causes good water quality, where there is control in nutrients available for both plant and animal species.While rice plant gain benefit from the uptake of nitrogen and phosphorous from fish excretes and unconsumed fish feed, fish, on the other hand serves as a biological control in the rice field, by eating insects and other natural prey in the water column, thereby reducing the application of fertilizer, pesticides, and herbicides (Akegbejo-Samsons, 2010; Bolay & Trpis, 1989;Rasowo et al., 2008).As such, the feed sources of fish are more diverse in the integrated RF than in fish ponds, which contributed to explain the better growth of fish in integrated RF compared to the fish monoculture.In another study, fish growth rate was found to be higher in the integrated RF compared to fish monoculture, which could be attributed to the higher phytoplankton biomass and insect concentrations which increased nutrient sources for fish in integrated RF compared to fish monoculture (Saowakoon et al., 2021).
The increase in FGR in the integrated RF was affected by the fish growth stage and rice varieties.

Oreochromis niloticus at the grow-out stage showed higher survival rate, hence better FGR than fish at the pre-grow out stage in the RF system (Jean-Renaud et al., 2016).In addition, rice varieties used in the RF system play a role in FGR, which was found to be significantly higher in the RF system using FARO60 than FARO45 rice varieties (Bello et al., 2020) possibly due to higher tillering capacity of FARO60 compared to FARO45, which may increase phytoplankton abundance.On the other hand, a close rice variety, FARO44, used in the RF system was found did not significantly reduced rice production but increased fish production and income of the farmers in the integrated RF system compared to the rice monoculture (Osuigwe et al., 2007).This shows the viability of these rice varieties to be used in the RF system.Added to this, this study has also discovered a wide variety of rice used in the RF system, including Wita 12, Djoukèmin, FARO44, ITA, BR11, and IR 2793-80-1, which could help to increase fish production and farmers' income in Africa (Jean-Renaud et al., 2016;Osuigwe et al., 2007;Rasowo et al., 2008;Rasowo & Auma, 2006).On another note, besides water quality, fish growth stage and rice varieties influencing fish growth and production, fish fed with external and/or natural food sources are also contributing to fish yield in the integrated RF system.The external food sources are processed and unprocessed food given by the farmer, including compound fish feed, inorganic fertilizer, corn meal, chicken yolk, and agricultural by-products (i.e.rice bran, rice straws, corn bran, poultry droppings) (Baba et al., 2013;Delphin et al., 2020;Mortillaro et al., 2022;Ofori et al., 2005;Serrem et al., 2015).While the natural food includes termites, azolla, and organisms available and populated as a result of natural fertilization from fish feces in the water ecosystem (e.g.phytoplankton, zooplankton, benthic algae, macroinvertebrates, decomposed weeds, mosquito larvae, insects, and small fishes) (Mortillaro et al., 2022;Niaré & Kalossi, 2014;Saowakoon et al., 2021;Serrem et al., 2015).Higher fish production would often require higher feed input (Hu et al., 2016).However, fish only assimilated 20-30% of nitrogen (Hu et al., 2016;Xie et al., 2011), indicating an increasing risk of environmental pollution from overfertilization and accumulation of nutrient in the rice field when fish are not harvested for a long time (Hu et al., 2016), nor does it take up by the rice plants.Therefore, to ensure sustainable fish and rice yield in Africa, critical farm planning should be made before integrating fish in the existing rice field system in SSA with consideration on soil fertility issues and possible environmental impacts.This can be achieved through capacity building by providing training to the farmers and empowering them with relevant knowledge and skills in integrated RF farming practices (Freed et al., 2023), thereby to avoid nutrient loss or wastage without increasing the use of chemical fertilizer and pesticides, causing additional cost inputs for the farmers and harm to the environment in the long-term period (Ge et al., 2010;Guo et al., 2022).

Lack of interest among the members of the Fish Farmers' Association of the Office du Niger in pursuing RF culture due to the limited access to irrigated land suitable for rice production, rice paddies land identified may not be conducive to fish production, and fear of losing soil fertility on the rice field.Other constraints on RF farming practices were water availability, short production (Continued )

purchase of fish fingerlings and fish feed, petrol for water pump, and net screen for guarding the fish from escaping (Desta et al., 2015;Nnaji et al., 2010).However, the costs of fertilizer and pesticides were reported to be reduced in the RF compared to rice monoculture because fish produces manure in the rice plot, which serves as natural fertilizers for soil fertilization (Nnaji et al., 2010;Yaro, 2003).Hence, the use of nitrogen fertilizers and pesticides are decreased in the integrated RF compared to rice monoculture (Hu et al., 2016;Nnaji et al., 2010).In one study, the cost of fertilizer and herbicide use were reduced by about 54% in the RF culture compared to rice culture alone (Nnaji et al., 2010).

Although the production costs increased on average by 300 USD/ha in the RF compared to rice monoculture, the increase in the total revenue was much higher (600 USD/ha) inducing an increase in farmers net income by 300 USD/ha.The higher net income in the RF could be explained by the higher price of fish and the higher contribution of fish to the total net income compared to rice.Therefore, the integrated RF has the potential to increase farmers' income and reduce poverty rate in farming dependent communities in Africa.

The type of fish species cultured in the integrated system also influenced the revenue generated.Catfish (Clarias or Heterobranchus sp.) contributed to most of the fish harvested and was accepted by most of the consumers, where it fetched higher price compared with tilapia.Besides, domesticated fish species had higher prices due to the bigger and standardized fish sizes compared to the captive wild fish introduced in the system.In addition, cultured fish are also found to have increased resistance to fish diseases and able to thrive well in extreme conditions due to the selective breeding carried out by the fish farmers.Another factor to consider is also a reliable source of fish fingerlings obtained from the fish hatchery.

The performance of integrated RF could also be affected by the environmental conditions.Farmer practicing RF system in different locations with an area of the rice plot double (1000 m 2 ) of the size of another plot (500 m 2 ) showed a slight difference in the average income (Ofori et al., 2005).This could be explained by the soil properties, weather and climate conditions influencing the rice and fish production in different localities of the area, suggesting the need to evaluate the suitable conditions for scaling integrated RF.Other factors influencing the performance of RF, which may need to be optimized include fish stocking density, and type of fish feed.

The selection of fish species to be cultured in the rice plot is also an important factor which affects farmers' income.A study by Akegbejo-Samsons (2010) has listed three potential fish species for integrated development in the rice field in Nigeria, tilapia (Sarotherodon melanotheron), catfish (Clarias longifilis), and mullet (Mugil cephalus).However, in other countries such as Ghana, Ethiopia, Mali, and Kenya, the Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) and African catfish (Clarias gariepinus) are the preferred species because of their higher ability to tolerate poor water quality, the availability of fish fry and the market demand (Dartey et al., 1999;Desta et al., 2015;Freed et al., 2023;Jean-Renaud et al., 2016;Niaré & Kalossi, 2014;Rasowo & Auma, 2006;Yaro, 2003).The selection of fish species is based on the current market prices of the cultured fish, ease of culture, availability of fish fry suited to be cultured in the environment, and the possibility to use the fish as biological control of other unwanted fish populations.Traditionally, some farmers will release catfish in the culture system to control overpopulation of tilapia fingerlings and serve to reduce feed costs (Freed et al., 2023).
Response of soil properties and environment to integrated RF system

The meta-analysis showed that soil properties in the integrated RF system were better enhanced than in rice culture alone (Desta et al., 2014;Serrem et al., 2015).The increase in these soil parameters (i.e.organic carbon and organic matter) indicates the benefits of changes in the physical and chemical properties of the soil due to the availability of fish in the integrated system.This is consistent with the findings in the RF culture by Arunrat et al. (2022) and Ji et al. (2023), which have also discovered SOC, organic matter, total nitrogen, available phosphorous, and clay content significantly higher in integrated RF than rice monoculture.Organic carbon storage in the soil is important on rice yield as it is associated with soil fertility, nutrient cycle, temperature, pH stability, and mitigation of greenhouse gases emissions (Arunrat & Pumijomnong, 2017;Ghimire et al., 2017;Lal et al., 2007).The accumulation of SOC was found directly affected by soil chemical and microbial activity, in which an increase in SOC content by 1 g kg −1 was reported to increase rice yield by 302 kg ha −1 (Arunrat et al., 2020;Ren et al., 2023).Comparing between integrated RF and rice monoculture, microbial community composition was found significantly different due to the difference in soil management practices of the RF and rice monoculture (Arunrat et al., 2022;Li et al., 2022;Zhao et al., 2021).The finding from the study discovered that genus Bacillus was found the most dominant in RF which plays an important role in nitrogen fixation and phosphorous nutrition for plant growth, indicating the benefits of integrated RF farming practices compared to the rice monoculture (Arunrat et al., 2022).This study showed that the integrated RF system increased dissolved oxygen (DO), pH, and phosphorus content, which is in line with the results of previous studies Hu et al. (2016); Jean-Renaud et al. (2016); Xie et al. (2011).Feces excreted by fish or from the unconsumed feed are recycled in the integrated system, where nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorous help to improve water productivity and soil fertility for fish growth and rice development (Hu et al., 2016;Jean-Renaud et al., 2016;Xie et al., 2011).In a study by Ge et al. (2010), it was found that a combination of organic and inorganic fertilizer is widely recommended to sustain agricultural production of the degraded soil fertility and quality in Asia and Africa.Therefore, the application of nutrients from fish waste or unconsumed feed and added with low use of fertilizer in the water environment could help to address the scarcity of inorganic fertilizers, the decline in soil fertility, and low rice yield, which affects rice production in SSA (Haefele et al., 2013;Johnson et al., 2023;Saito et al., 2023;Tsujimoto et al., 2019).On the other hand, while chemical fertilizers are typically used by farmers to increase crop production, contributing to 30-50% of crop yield (Song et al., 2022), a continuous application and excessive use of chemical or inorganic fertilizer alone was reported to negatively affect the environment, decrease soil productivity, reduce soil pH and NUE, which in return affecting crop yield and soil health in the long term than organic fertilizers (Ge et al., 2010;Guo et al., 2022;Kai et al., 2020;Liu et al., 2021).Organic fertilizer including fish waste could help to improve soil structure and physical characteristics, NUE, soil fertility, increase organic matter, and enhance soil microbial community and diversity, serving as a key factor in restoring and maintaining soil health to improve fish and rice yield (Arunrat et al., 2022;Cai et al., 2024;Liu et al., 2021;Ren et al., 2023).

Besides that, the increasing use of pesticides in Africa in controlling pest was reported bringing hazardous implication on both target and non-target organisms where some enter the food chain (Sankoh et al., 2016).Insecticides, organochlorine, and organophosphorus pesticides for example, can accumulate in soil and sediments, and in the tissues of both plant and animal, including fish species, which may further cause risk on human health (El-Alfy et al., 2019;Metwally et al., 2023;Sankoh et al., 2016).It can also be transported and spread along the food chain by water and air, potentially posing threats to other environments that are far from the contamination point (Sankoh et al., 2016;USAID, 2009).Therefore, to counter the negative impacts from using fertilizers and pesticides in the field, integrated RF farming can provide a sustainable natural and environment friendly solution through lowering of these chemical usage (Berg & Tam, 2018), while maintaining water productivity and soil fertility for both fish and rice growth (Ge et al., 2010;Hu et al., 2016).

In addition, the types of RF integration practiced by the farmer also affect soil quality, water productivity and environment in general.It was found that three types of integrated RF systems were practiced in Africa.This includes concurrent RF culture (CRF), concurrent RF culture with manured sump (CRF-M), and RF culture with fish refuge (RF-FR), with RF production practices depend on rainfed, irrigated, or submerged water (Baba et al., 2013;Dartey et al., 1999;Freed et al., 2023;Jean-Renaud et al., 2016;Rasowo et al., 2008;Rasowo & Auma, 2006;Ssanyu et al., 2011).Ponds given organic manures provide a more favourable environment for fish and rice growth by improving water productivity and soil properties.Similarly, farms practicing RF-FR also showed better fish and rice yield compared with the rice monoculture, because uneaten fish feed and fecal matter from fish fertilize the water and soil, thus promoting a favourable environment for both fish and crop growth (Baba et al., 2013;Desta et al., 2015;Hu et al., 2016;Rasowo et al., 2008;Rasowo & Auma, 2006).Study by Mortillaro et al. (2022) showed that supplying RF culture system with organic fertilizers improves natural productivity in the system, which provides food for the fish and increases soil fertility for rice growth.In the same study, analysis on common carp fish feeding behaviour using stable carbon and nitrogen isotopes found changes in 45-day-old fish fry feeding sources from external sources (i.e.chicken yolk and corn meal) to natural food sources, assumed to be mainly from detritus, plants, and invertebrates, after 100 days of fish growing period.From the gut content analyses of common carp, it was revealed of a wide variety of forage food consumed, including phytoplankton, zooplankton, periphyton, decomposed weeds, mosquito larvae, and macroinvertebrates, suggesting the importance of organic fertilization that enhances ecological productivity in the integrated RF system for both fish and rice production (Mortillaro et al., 2022).Despite varied diet composition in the stomach content in many fish species throughout the culture period, the food items consumed were similar among all fish species, including herbivorous, omnivorous, and carnivorous fish species, such as Oreochromis niloticus, Cyprinus carpio and Channa striata, with insects dominated the diet of all fishes and differ in second preference to phytoplankton, benthic algae, and zooplankton (Saowakoon et al., 2021).The deposit of organic fertilizers from fish wastes contributed to soil fertility regeneration with fish feeding on natural food such as insects, weeds, and zooplankton available in the water (Delphin et al., 2020;Mortillaro et al., 2022;Simon & Benhamou, 2009).In all the studies reported, it was observed that most farms fertilized their rice field ponds with agricultural by-products and provide feed, mainly rice bran, to the fish.These are based on past experiences, showing that these management practices were recommended to be used in the RF system.

Concerning the higher prevalence of malaria to the communities living in rice growing villages in Africa (Chan et al., 2022), RF farming could serve to help reduce mosquitoes with the possibility to eliminate them in the rice field where it was eaten by the fish (Bolay & Trpis, 1989).In addition, RF culture system supplemented with or without food were generally found increasing plankton species richness and density (Delphin et al., 2020;Mortillaro et al., 2022;Ssanyu et al., 2011).Freed et al. (2023) described this system as a community fish refuge (CFR) approach, with improved perennial aquatic habitats and enhanced floodplain habitat for fish production.
Conclusion

This study evaluated the impacts of the RF on water quality parameters, rice yield, fish growth rates, and profitability through a combined meta-analysis and literature review in Africa.The results showed that RF integration significantly increased FGR, production cost and farmer's income compared to the rice or fish monoculture in selected African countries.Rice yield was similar in integrated RF and rice monoculture.Several factors were found to influence FGR and farmer's income in the integrated RF system, including the initial size of fish at stocking, rice varieties, quality of fish fingerlings, type of fish feed given, type of RF system, soil properties, fish stocking density, and fish species.A strong correlation was found between water pH and DO, and between water pH, DO and rice yield in the integrated RF system, suggesting the benefits of fish addition into the system which helps to improve soil fertility and water quality, leading to increase in fish and rice production.Other benefits of RF system reported include improved water use efficiency and nutrient use efficiency, control of weeds, pests, and diseases, and adaptation to climate change.Constraints affecting the adoption of integrated RF system in Africa include land ownership, water supply, access to fish feed, price and quality of fingerlings and fish feed, as well as lack of funding.The findings from this study suggest the integrated RF system as a potential climate-smart agriculture (CSA) strategy for sustainable food production in Africa, by improving food and nutrition security through greater production and diversification, thereby increasing income, and promoting environmental benefits.More field observations and long-term monitoring are necessary to conclusively confirm the findings from the limited data identified in this study.Hence, further studies should be conducted on land suitability for integrated RF and management practices to optimize input use efficiency and increase rice yield, fish growth and farmers' income.
